nodes.name: Reduction strategy
nodes.statement: Intuitively, a reduction strategy is an algorithm that, for a given term, chooses the redex to contract if several redexes appear in the term.
differentia: for a given term, chooses the redex to contract if several redexes appear in the term

nodes.name: Normalising reduction strategy
nodes.statement: A reduction strategy is \emph{normalising} if following the strategy will, if at all possible, eventually lead to a normal form: a term containing no redexes.
differentia: following the strategy will, if at all possible, eventually lead to a normal form

nodes.name: Ordinal notation
nodes.statement: Moreover, we denote the first infinite ordinal by $\omega$, and arbitrary ordinals by $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, and so on.

nodes.name: Natural numbers
nodes.statement: We use $\mathbb{N}$ to denote the set of natural numbers, starting from zero.

nodes.name: Signature
nodes.statement: We assume a signature $\Sigma$, each element of which has finite arity.

nodes.name: Meta-terms (informal)
nodes.statement: The (infinite) \emph{meta-terms} are defined informally in a top-down fashion by the following rules, where $s$ and $s_1$, \ldots, $s_n$ are again meta-terms: \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \item each variable $x$ is a meta-term, \item if $x$ is a variable and $s$ is a finite meta-term, then $[x] s$ is a meta-term, \item if $Z$ is a meta-variable of arity $n$, then $Z(s_1, \ldots, s_n)$ is a meta-term, \item if $f \in \Sigma$ has arity $n$, then $f(s_1, \ldots, s_n)$ is a meta-term.
nodes.statement_short: Meta-terms built top-down from variables, abstractions $[x]s$, meta-variable applications and function symbols.

nodes.name: Abstraction
nodes.statement: A meta-term of the form $[x] s$ is called an \emph{abstraction}.

nodes.name: Bound variable and scope
nodes.statement: Each occurrence of the variable $x$ in $s$ is \emph{bound} in $[x]s$, and each subterm of $s$ is said to occur in the \emph{scope} of the abstraction.

nodes.name: Root symbol
nodes.statement: If $s$ is a meta-term, we denote by $\rs{s}$ the root symbol of $s$. Following the definition of meta-terms, we define $\rs{x} = x$, $\rs{[x]s} = [x]$, $\rs{Z(s_1, \ldots, s_n)} = Z$, and $\rs{f(s_1, \ldots, s_n)} = f$.

nodes.name: Terms
nodes.statement: The set of \emph{terms} is defined as the set of all meta-terms without meta-variables.

nodes.name: Context and one-hole context
nodes.statement: Moreover, a \emph{context} is defined as a meta-term over $\Sigma \cup \{ \Box \}$ where $\Box$ is a fresh nullary function symbol and a \emph{one-hole} context is a context in which precisely one $\Box$ occurs.

nodes.name: Hole filling C[s]
nodes.statement: If $C[\Box]$ is a one-hole context and $s$ is a term, we obtain a term by replacing $\Box$ by s; the new term is denoted by $C[s]$.

nodes.name: Capture avoidance disallowed for contexts
nodes.statement: Capture avoidance is disallowed for contexts as we do not want to lose variable bindings over rewrite steps in case: (i) an abstraction occurs in a context, and (ii) a variable bound by the abstraction occurs in a subterm being rewritten. Note that this means that the representative employed as the context must already be fixed \emph{before} performing the actual rewrite step. As motivation, consider $\lambda$-calculus: In the term $\lambda x . (\lambda y . x) z$, contracting the redex inside the context $\lambda x . \Box$ yields $\lambda x.x$, whence the substitution rules for contexts should be such that \[ (\lambda x. \Box)\{(\lambda y . x) z / \Box\} \rightarrow_\beta \lambda x.x \, . \] If capture avoidance were in effect for contexts, we would have an $\alpha$-conversion in the rewrite step, whence \[ (\lambda x .\Box)\{(\lambda y . x) z / \Box\} \rightarrow_\beta \lambda w . x \, , \] which is clearly wrong.
nodes.statement_short: Contexts use fixed representatives so that variable bindings are not lost by rewriting inside a context, illustrated with $\lambda$-calculus.

nodes.name: Meta-terms as metric completion
nodes.statement: Formally, meta-terms are defined by taking the metric completion of the set of finite meta-terms, the set inductively defined by the rules presented earlier.

nodes.name: Distance between terms
nodes.statement: The distance between two terms is either taken as $0$, if the terms are $\alpha$-equivalent, or as $2^{-k}$ with $k$ the minimal depth at which the terms differ, also taking into account $\alpha$-equivalence.

nodes.name: Meta-terms and distances
nodes.statement: Any finite meta-term, e.g.\ $[x]Z(x,f(x))$, is a meta-term. We also have that $Z'(Z'(Z'(\ldots)))$ is a meta-term, as is $Z_1([x_1]x_1,Z_2([x_2]x_2,\ldots))$. The meta-terms $[x]Z(x,f(x))$ and $[y]Z(y,f(y))$ have distance $0$ and the meta-terms $[x]Z(x,f(x))$ and $[y]Z(y,f(z))$ have distance $\frac{1}{8}$.

nodes.name: Set of positions
nodes.statement: Given a meta-term $s$, its \emph{set of positions}, denoted $\pos{s}$, is the set of finite strings over $\mathbb{N}$, with $\epsilon$ the empty string, such that: \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \item if $s = x$ for some variable $x$, then $\pos{s} = \{ \epsilon \}$, \item if $s = [x] t$, then $\pos{s} = \{ \epsilon \} \cup \{ 0 \cdot p \; | \; p \in \pos{t} \}$, \item if $s = Z(t_1, \ldots, t_n)$, then $\pos{s} = \{ \epsilon \} \cup \{ i \cdot p \; | \; 1 \leq i \leq n, \, p \in \pos{t_i} \}$, \item if $s = f(t_1, \ldots, t_n)$, then $\pos{s} = \{ \epsilon \} \cup \{ i \cdot p \; | \; 1 \leq i \leq n, \, p \in \pos{t_i} \}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Positions of a meta-term: finite strings over $\mathbb{N}$ defined top-down, with $\epsilon$ the root.

nodes.name: Depth of a position
nodes.statement: The \emph{depth} of a position $p$, denoted $\vert p \vert$, is the number of characters in $p$.

nodes.name: Prefix of a position
nodes.statement: Given $p, \, q \in \pos{s}$, we write $p \leq q$ and say that $p$ is a \emph{prefix} of $q$, if there exists an $r \in \pos{s}$ such that $p \cdot r = q$.

nodes.name: Strict prefix
nodes.statement: If $r \not = \epsilon$, we also write $p < q$ and say that the prefix is \emph{strict}.

nodes.name: Subterm at a position
nodes.statement: We denote by $s|_p$ the subterm of $s$ that \emph{occurs at position} $p \in \pos{s}$.

nodes.name: Subterm above a position
nodes.statement: Moreover, if $q \in \pos{s}$ and $p < q$, we say that the subterm at position $p$ occurs \emph{above} $q$.

nodes.name: Subterm below a position
nodes.statement: Finally, if $p > q$, then we say that the subterm occurs \emph{below} $q$.

nodes.name: Chain
nodes.statement: Let $s$ be a meta-term. A \emph{chain} in $s$ is a sequence of (context, position)-pairs $(C_i[\Box],p_i)_{i < \alpha}$, with $\alpha \leq \omega$, such that for each $(C_i[\Box], p_i)$: \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \item if $i + 1 < \alpha$, then $C_i[\Box]$ has \emph{one} hole and $C_i[t_i] = s|_{p_i}$ for some term $t_i$, and \item if $i + 1 = \alpha$, then $C_i[\Box]$ has \emph{no} holes and $C_i[\Box] = s|_{p_i}$, \end{enumerate} and such that $p_{i+1} = p_i \cdot q_i$ for all $i + 1 < \alpha$ where $q_i$ is the position of the hole in $C_i[\Box]$. If $\alpha < \omega$, respectively $\alpha = \omega$, then the chain is called \emph{finite}, respectively \emph{infinite}.
nodes.statement_short: A chain in a meta-term is a (finite or infinite) sequence of contexts nested right below each other.

nodes.name: Vector shorthand
nodes.statement: Below, we use $\vec{x}$ and $\vec{t}$ as short-hands for, respectively, the sequences $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ and $t_1, \ldots, t_n$ with $n \geq 0$.

nodes.name: Substitution
nodes.statement: A \emph{substitution} of the terms $\vec{t}$ for distinct variables $\vec{x}$ in a term $s$, denoted $s[\vec{x} := \vec{t}]$, is defined as: \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \item $x_i[\vec{x} := \vec{t}] = t_i$, \item $y[\vec{x} := \vec{t}] = y$, if $y$ does not occur in $\vec{x}$, \item $([y]s')[\vec{x} := \vec{t}] = [y](s'[\vec{x} := \vec{t}])$, \item $f(s_1, \ldots, s_m)[\vec{x} := \vec{t}] = f(s_1[\vec{x} := \vec{t}], \ldots, s_m[\vec{x} := \vec{t}])$. \end{enumerate} The above definition implicitly takes into account the usual variable convention \cite{B85} in the third clause to avoid the binding of free variables by the abstraction. We now define substitutes (adopting this name from Kahrs \cite{K93}) and valuations.
nodes.statement_short: Simultaneous substitution $s[\vec{x} := \vec{t}]$ of terms for distinct variables, defined clause-wise.
nodes.label: defsubstitution

nodes.name: Substitute
nodes.statement: An \emph{$n$-ary substitute} is a mapping denoted $\underline{\lambda} x_1, \ldots, x_n . s$ or $\underline{\lambda} \vec{x} . s$, with $s$ a term, such that: \begin{equation} (\underline{\lambda} \vec{x} . s)(t_1, \ldots, t_n) = s[\vec{x} := \vec{t}] \, . \end{equation}
nodes.label: defsubstitute

nodes.name: Substitute application (parallel beta)
nodes.statement: (\underline{\lambda} \vec{x} . s)(t_1, \ldots, t_n) = s[\vec{x} := \vec{t}] \, .
nodes.label: pbetaeq

nodes.name: Valuation
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma$ be a function that maps meta-variables to substitutes such that, for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, if $Z$ has arity $n$, then so does $\sigma(Z)$. A \emph{valuation} induced by $\sigma$ is a relation $\bar{\sigma}$ that takes meta-terms to terms such that: \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \item $\bar{\sigma}(x) = x$, \item $\bar{\sigma}([x]s) = [x](\bar{\sigma}(s))$, \item $\bar{\sigma}(Z(s_1, \ldots, s_m)) = \sigma(Z)(\bar{\sigma}(s_1), \ldots, \bar{\sigma}(s_m))$, \item $\bar{\sigma}(f(s_1, \ldots, s_m)) = f(\bar{\sigma}(s_1), \ldots, \bar{\sigma}(s_m))$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A valuation $\bar{\sigma}$ induced by a map from meta-variables to substitutes, applied clause-wise to meta-terms.
nodes.label: defvaluation

nodes.name: Finite chains property
nodes.statement: Let $s$ be a meta-term. A \emph{chain of meta-variables} in $s$ is a chain in $s$, written $(C_i[\Box],p_i)_{i < \alpha}$ with $\alpha \leq \omega$, such that for each $i < \alpha$ it is the case that $C_i[\Box] = Z(t_1, \ldots, t_n)$ with $t_j = \Box$ for exactly one $1 \leq j \leq n$. The meta-term $s$ is said to satisfy the \emph{finite chains property} if no infinite chain of meta-variables occurs in $s$.

nodes.name: Finite chains property examples
nodes.statement: The meta-term $[x_1]Z_1([x_2]Z_2(\ldots [x_n]Z_n(\ldots)))$ satisfies the finite chains property. The meta-terms $Z(Z(\ldots Z(\ldots)))$ and $Z_1(Z_2(\ldots Z_n(\ldots)))$ do not.

nodes.name: Valuations on meta-terms with finite chains property
nodes.statement: Let $s$ be a meta-term satisfying the finite chains property and let $\bar{\sigma}$ a valuation. There is a unique term that is the result of applying $\bar{\sigma}$ to $s$. \qed
assumptions: $s$ be a meta-term satisfying the finite chains property
$\bar{\sigma}$ a valuation
conclusions: There is a unique term that is the result of applying $\bar{\sigma}$ to $s$.
nodes.label: prop:metasane

nodes.name: Pattern and closed meta-term
nodes.statement: A finite meta-term is a \emph{pattern} if each of its meta-variables has distinct bound variables as its arguments. Moreover, a meta-term is \emph{closed} if all its variables occur bound.

nodes.name: Rewrite rule and iCRS
nodes.statement: A \emph{rewrite rule} is a pair $(l, r)$, denoted $l \rightarrow r$, where $l$ is a finite meta-term and $r$ is a meta-term, such that: \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \item $l$ is a pattern with a function symbol at the root, \item all meta-variables that occur in $r$ also occur in $l$, \item $l$ and $r$ are closed, and \item $r$ satisfies the finite chains property. \end{enumerate} The meta-terms $l$ and $r$ are called, respectively, the \emph{left-hand side} and the \emph{right-hand side} of the rewrite rule. An \emph{infinitary Combinatory Reduction System (iCRS)} is a pair $\trsp{C}{\Sigma}{R}$ with $\Sigma$ a signature and $R$ a set of rewrite rules.
nodes.statement_short: A rewrite rule $l \rightarrow r$ has a finite pattern lhs and closed rhs with the finite chains property; an iCRS is a signature with a set of rules.

nodes.name: Rewrite step, redex and redex pattern
nodes.statement: A \emph{rewrite step} is a pair of terms $(s, t)$, denoted $s \rightarrow t$, adorned with a one-hole context $C[\Box]$, a rewrite rule $l \rightarrow r$, and a valuation $\bar{\sigma}$ such that $s = C[\bar{\sigma}(l)]$ and $t = C[\bar{\sigma}(r)]$. The term $\bar{\sigma}(l)$ is called an \emph{$l \rightarrow r$-redex}, or simply a \emph{redex}. The redex \emph{occurs} at position $p$ and depth $|p|$ in $s$, where $p$ is the position of the hole in $C[\Box]$. A position $q$ of $s$ is said to occur in the \emph{redex pattern} of the redex at position $p$ if $q \geq p$ and if there does not exist a position $q'$ with $q \geq p \cdot q'$ such that $q'$ is the position of a meta-variable in $l$.

nodes.name: Left-linear
nodes.statement: A rewrite rule is \emph{left-linear}, if each meta-variable occurs at most once in its left-hand side. Moreover, an iCRS is \emph{left-linear} if all its rewrite rules are.

nodes.name: Overlap and orthogonal iCRS
nodes.statement: Let $s$ and $t$ be finite meta-terms that have no meta-variables in common. The meta-term $s$ \emph{overlaps} $t$ if there exists a non-meta-variable position $p \in \pos{s}$ and a valuation $\bar{\sigma}$ such that $\bar{\sigma}(s|_p) = \bar{\sigma}(t)$. Two rewrite rules \emph{overlap} if their left-hand sides overlap and if the overlap does not occur at the root when two copies of the same rule are considered. An iCRS is \emph{orthogonal} if all its rewrite rules are left-linear and no two (possibly the same) rewrite rules overlap.

nodes.name: Overlap position is not a bound variable
nodes.statement: In case the rewrite rules $l_1 \rightarrow r_1$ and $l_2 \rightarrow r_2$ overlap at position $p$, it follows that $p$ cannot be the position of a bound variable in $l_1$. If it were, we would obtain for some valuation $\bar{\sigma}$ and variable $x$ that $\bar{\sigma}(l_1|_p) = x = \bar{\sigma}(l_2)$, which would imply that $l_2$ does not have a function symbol at the root, as required by the definition of rewrite rules.

nodes.name: Finite overlap witness
nodes.statement: Moreover, it is easily seen that if two left-linear rules overlap in an infinite term, there is also a finite term in which they overlap.
assumptions: two left-linear rules overlap in an infinite term
conclusions: there is also a finite term in which they overlap

nodes.name: Fully-extended
nodes.statement: A pattern is \emph{fully-extended} \cite{HP96,O96}, if, for each of its meta-variables $Z$ and each abstraction $[x]s$ having an occurrence of $Z$ in its scope, $x$ is an argument of that occurrence of $Z$. Moreover, a rewrite rule is \emph{fully-extended} if its left-hand side is and an iCRS is \emph{fully-extended} if all its rewrite rules are.
nodes.label: def:fully_extended

nodes.name: Fully-extended patterns
nodes.statement: The pattern $f(g([x]Z(x)))$ is fully-extended. Hence, so is the rewrite rule $f(g([x]Z(x))) \rightarrow h([x]Z(x))$. The pattern $g([x]f(Z(x),Z'))$, with $Z'$ occurring in the scope of the abstraction $[x]$, is not fully-extended as $x$ does not occur as an argument of $Z'$.

nodes.name: Transfinite reduction; weak continuity and convergence
nodes.statement: A \emph{transfinite reduction} with domain $\alpha > 0$ is a sequence of terms $(s_\beta)_{\beta < \alpha}$ adorned with a rewrite step $s_\beta \rightarrow s_{\beta + 1}$ for each $\beta + 1 < \alpha$. In case $\alpha = \alpha' + 1$, the reduction is \emph{closed} and of length $\alpha'$. In case $\alpha$ is a limit ordinal, the reduction is called \emph{open} and of length $\alpha$. The reduction is \emph{weakly continuous} or \emph{Cauchy continuous} if, for every limit ordinal $\gamma < \alpha$, the distance between $s_\beta$ and $s_\gamma$ tends to $0$ as $\beta$ approaches $\gamma$ from below. The reduction is \emph{weakly convergent} or \emph{Cauchy convergent} if it is weakly continuous and closed.
nodes.statement_short: Transfinite reductions indexed by ordinals; open/closed, and weakly continuous/convergent when terms Cauchy-converge at limits.

nodes.name: Strongly continuous / convergent reduction
nodes.statement: Let $(s_\beta)_{\beta < \alpha}$ be a transfinite reduction. For each rewrite step $s_\beta \rightarrow s_{\beta + 1}$, let $d_\beta$ denote the depth of the contracted redex. The reduction is \emph{strongly continuous} if it is weakly continuous and if, for every limit ordinal $\gamma < \alpha$, the depth $d_\beta$ tends to infinity as $\beta$ approaches $\gamma$ from below. The reduction is \emph{strongly convergent} if strongly continuous and closed.

nodes.name: Weakly vs strongly convergent reductions
nodes.statement: Consider the rewrite rule $f([x]Z(x)) \rightarrow Z(f([x]Z(x)))$ and observe that $f([x]x) \rightarrow f([x]x)$. Define $s_\beta = f([x]x)$ for all $\beta < \omega \cdot 2$. The reduction $(s_\beta)_{\beta < \omega \cdot 2}$, where in each step we contract the redex at the root, is open and weakly continuous. Adding the term $f([x]x)$ to the end of the reduction yields a weakly convergent reduction. Both reductions are of length $\omega \cdot 2$. The above reduction is not strongly continuous as all contracted redexes occur at the root, i.e.\ at depth $0$. In addition, it cannot be extended to a strongly convergent reduction. However, the reduction \[ f([x]g(x)) \rightarrow g(f([x]g(x)) \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow g^n(f([x]g(x))) \rightarrow g^{n + 1}(f([x]g(x))) \rightarrow \cdots \] is open and strongly continuous. Extending the reduction with the term $g^\omega$, where $g^\omega$ is shorthand for the infinite term $g(g(\ldots g(\ldots)))$, yields a strongly convergent reduction. Both reductions are of length $\omega$.
nodes.statement_short: A root-rewriting reduction that is weakly but not strongly convergent, versus one converging strongly to $g^\omega$.
nodes.label: ex:wconv

nodes.name: Reduction notation
nodes.statement: By $s \trewtp{\alpha} t$, respectively $s \trewtp{\leq \alpha} t$, we denote a \emph{strongly convergent} reduction of ordinal length $\alpha$, respectively of ordinal length at most $\alpha$. By $s \twoheadrightarrow t$ we denote a \emph{strongly convergent} reduction of arbitrary ordinal length and by $s \rightarrow^* t$ we denote a reduction of finite length. Reductions are usually ranged over by capital letters such as $D$, $E$, $S$, and $T$. The concatenation of reductions $S$ and $T$ is denoted by $S ; T$.

nodes.name: Concatenation of strongly convergent reductions
nodes.statement: Note that the concatenation of any finite number of strongly convergent reductions yields a strongly convergent reduction.
conclusions: the concatenation of any finite number of strongly convergent reductions yields a strongly convergent reduction

nodes.name: Finitely many steps above any depth
nodes.statement: If $s \twoheadrightarrow t$, then the number of steps contracting redexes at depths less than $d \in \mathbb{N}$ is finite for any $d$ and $s \twoheadrightarrow t$ has countable length.
assumptions: $s \twoheadrightarrow t$
conclusions: the number of steps contracting redexes at depths less than $d \in \mathbb{N}$ is finite for any $d$
$s \twoheadrightarrow t$ has countable length
nodes.label: depthlem

nodes.name: Compression Lemma
nodes.statement: For every fully-extended, left-linear iCRS, if $s \trewtp{\alpha} t$, then $s \trewtp{\leq \omega} t$. \qed
assumptions: For every fully-extended, left-linear iCRS
$s \trewtp{\alpha} t$
conclusions: $s \trewtp{\leq \omega} t$
nodes.label: the:compression

nodes.name: Descendants and residuals
nodes.statement: The twin notions of \emph{descendants} and \emph{residuals} formalise, respectively, ``what happens'' to positions and redexes across reductions. Across a rewrite step, the only positions that can have descendants are those that occur outside the redex pattern of the contracted redex and that are not positions of the variables bound by abstractions in the redex pattern. Across a reduction, the definition of descendants follows the notion of a descendant across a rewrite step, employing strong convergence in the limit ordinal case.

nodes.name: Descendant and residual notation
nodes.statement: Let $s \twoheadrightarrow t$. Assume $P \subseteq \pos{s}$ and $\mathcal{U}$ a set of redexes in $s$. We denote the descendants of $P$ across $s \twoheadrightarrow t$ by $P/(s \twoheadrightarrow t)$ and the residuals of $\mathcal{U}$ across $s \twoheadrightarrow t$ by $\mathcal{U}/(s \twoheadrightarrow t)$. Moreover, if $P = \{ p \}$ and $\mathcal{U} = \{ u \}$, then we also write $p/(s \twoheadrightarrow t)$ and $u/(s \twoheadrightarrow t)$. Finally, if $s \twoheadrightarrow t$ consists of a single step contracting a redex $u$, then we sometimes write~$\mathcal{U}/u$.

nodes.name: Orthogonality in Section 2.4
nodes.statement: Assuming in the remainder of this section that every iCRS is \emph{orthogonal} and that $s$ is a term and $\mathcal{U}$ a set of redexes in $s$, we first define developments:

nodes.name: Development; complete and finite developments
nodes.statement: A \emph{development} of $\mathcal{U}$ is a strongly convergent reduction such that each step contracts a residual of a redex in $\mathcal{U}$. A development $s \twoheadrightarrow t$ is called \emph{complete} if $\mathcal{U}/(s \twoheadrightarrow t) = \emptyset$. Moreover, a development is called $\emph{finite}$ if $s \twoheadrightarrow t$ is finite.

nodes.name: Complete developments need not exist
nodes.statement: A complete development of a set of redexes does not necessarily exist in the infinite case. Consider for example the rule $f(Z) \rightarrow Z$ and the term $f^\omega$. The set of all redexes in $f^\omega$ does not have a complete development: After any (partial) development a residual of a redex in $f^\omega$ always remains at the root of the resulting term. Hence, any complete development will have an infinite number of root-steps and thus will not be strongly convergent.
nodes.statement_short: With $f(Z) \rightarrow Z$ the redexes of $f^\omega$ have no complete development, since infinitely many root steps would be needed.

nodes.name: Complete development notation
nodes.statement: Although complete developments do not always exist, the following results can still be obtained \cite{JJ05b}, where we write $s \Rightarrow^\mathcal{U} t$ for the reduction $s \twoheadrightarrow t$ if it is a complete development of the set of redexes $\mathcal{U}$ in $s$.

nodes.name: Complete developments persist across developments
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{U}$ has a complete development and if $s \twoheadrightarrow t$ is a (not necessarily complete) development of $\mathcal{U}$, then $\mathcal{U}/(s \twoheadrightarrow t)$ has a complete development. \qed
assumptions: $\mathcal{U}$ has a complete development
$s \twoheadrightarrow t$ is a (not necessarily complete) development of $\mathcal{U}$
conclusions: $\mathcal{U}/(s \twoheadrightarrow t)$ has a complete development
nodes.label: cdacrossd

nodes.name: Finite sets have finite complete developments
nodes.statement: Let $s$ be a term and $\mathcal{U}$ a set of redexes in $s$. If $\mathcal{U}$ is finite, then it has a finite complete development. \qed
assumptions: $s$ be a term and $\mathcal{U}$ a set of redexes in $s$
$\mathcal{U}$ is finite
conclusions: it has a finite complete development
nodes.label: lem:finite_dev

nodes.name: Projection of finite developments over complete developments
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{V}$ be sets of redexes in $s$ such that $\mathcal{U}$ has a complete development $s \Rightarrow t$ and $\mathcal{V}$ is finite. The following diagram commutes: \[ \xymatrix{ s \ar@{=>}[r]^{\mathcal{V}} \ar@{=>}[d]^{\mathcal{U}} & t' \ar@{=>}[d]^{\mathcal{U}/(s \Rightarrow^\mathcal{V} t')} \\ t \ar@{=>}[r]_{\mathcal{V}/(s \Rightarrow^\mathcal{U} t)} & s' } \]
assumptions: $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{V}$ be sets of redexes in $s$ such that $\mathcal{U}$ has a complete development $s \Rightarrow t$ and $\mathcal{V}$ is finite
conclusions: The following diagram commutes:
nodes.statement_short: If $\mathcal{U}$ has a complete development and $\mathcal{V}$ is finite, the developments of $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{V}$ and their residuals form a commuting square.
nodes.label: prop:finite_over_normal

nodes.name: Projection D/u of a finite sequence of complete developments
nodes.statement: Finally, if the reduction $D$ consists of a finite number of complete developments $\fscd{s}{U}{n}$ and if $s_0 \rightarrow t_0$ contracts a redex $u$, then $D / u$ denotes the reduction $\fscd{t}{V}{n}$, where $\mathcal{V}_i = \mathcal{U}_i / (s_{i - 1} \Rightarrow t_{i - 1})$ for all $0 < i \leq n$ with $s_{i - 1} \Rightarrow t_{i - 1}$ a complete development of the residuals of $u$ in $s_{i - 1}$. Written as a diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ s_0 \ar@{=>}[r]^{\mathcal{U}_1} \ar[d]^{u} & s_1 \ar@{=>}[r]^{\mathcal{U}_2} \ar@{=>}[d] & \cdot \ar@{.}[r] \ar@{=>}[d] & \cdot \ar@{=>}[r]^{\mathcal{U}_n} & s_n \ar@{=>}[d]^{u/D} \\ t_0 \ar@{=>}[r]_{\mathcal{V}_1} & t_1 \ar@{=>}[r]_{\mathcal{V}_2} & \cdot \ar@{.}[r] & \cdot \ar@{=>}[r]_{\mathcal{V}_n} & t_n } \]
nodes.statement_short: $D/u$ projects a finite sequence of complete developments over a step $u$ by developing residuals tile by tile.

nodes.name: Existence of D/u for finite developments
nodes.statement: The existence of $D / u$ depends on the existence of the complete developments that define the reduction. By Proposition \ref{prop:finite_over_normal}, existence is guaranteed in case $\mathcal{U}_i$ is finite for all $0 < i < n$.
assumptions: in case $\mathcal{U}_i$ is finite for all $0 < i < n$
conclusions: existence is guaranteed

nodes.name: Redex position notation
nodes.statement: Assuming a term $s$ in an \emph{orthogonal} iCRS and a set $\mathcal{U}$ of redexes in $s$, we first define paths and path projections, where we denote by $\redpos{u}$ the position of the redex $u$ in $s$.

nodes.name: Variable bound by a redex
nodes.statement: Moreover, we say that a variable $x$ is \emph{bound by a redex} $u$ if $x$ is bound by an abstraction $[x]$ which occurs in the left-hand side of the rewrite rule employed in $u$.

nodes.name: Path
nodes.statement: A \emph{path} of $s$ with respect to $\mathcal{U}$ is a sequence of alternating nodes and edges. Each node is labelled either $(s, p)$ with $p \in \pos{s}$ or $(r, p, \redpos{u})$ with $r$ the right-hand side of a rewrite rule, $p \in \pos{r}$, and $u \in \mathcal{U}$. Each edge is directed and either unlabelled or labelled with an element of $\mathbb{N}$. Every path starts with a node labelled $(s, \epsilon)$. If a node $n$ of a path is labelled $(s, p)$ and has an outgoing edge to a node $n'$, then: \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \item if $s|_p$ is neither a redex in $\mathcal{U}$ nor a variable bound by a redex in $\mathcal{U}$, then for some $i \in \pos{s|_p} \cap \mathbb{N}$ the node $n'$ is labelled $(s, p \cdot i)$ and the edge from $n$ to $n'$ is labelled~$i$, \item if $s|_p$ is a redex $u \in \mathcal{U}$ with $l \rightarrow r$ the employed rewrite rule, then the node $n'$ is labelled $(r, \epsilon, \redpos{u})$ and the edge from $n$ to $n'$ is unlabelled, \item if $s|_p$ is a variable $x$ bound by a redex $u \in \mathcal{U}$ with $l \rightarrow r$ the employed rewrite rule, then the node $n'$ is labelled $(r, p' \cdot i, \redpos{u})$ and the edge from $n$ to $n'$ is unlabelled, such that $(r, p', \redpos{u})$ was the last node before $n$ with $\redpos{u}$, $\rs{r|_{p'}} = Z$, and $l|_{q \cdot i} = x$ with $q$ the unique position of $Z$ in $l$. \end{enumerate} If a node $n$ of a path is labelled $(r, p, \redpos{u})$ and has an outgoing edge to a node $n'$, then: \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \item if $\rs{r|_p}$ is not a meta-variable, then for some $i \in \pos{r|_p} \cap \mathbb{N}$ the node $n'$ is labelled $(r, p \cdot i, \redpos{u})$ and the edge from $n$ to $n'$ is labelled $i$, \item if $\rs{r|_p}$ is a meta-variable $Z$, then the node $n'$ is labelled $(s, \redpos{u} \cdot q)$ and the edge from $n$ to $n'$ is unlabelled, such that $l \rightarrow r$ is the rewrite rule employed in $u$ and such that $q$ is the unique position of $Z$ in $l$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.genus: sequence of alternating nodes and edges
nodes.statement_short: A path of $s$ w.r.t. $\mathcal{U}$ walks top-down through $s$, jumping into rule right-hand sides at redexes and back at meta-variables.

nodes.name: Maximal path
nodes.statement: We say that a path is \emph{maximal} if it is not a proper prefix of another path.

nodes.name: Path notation
nodes.statement: We write a path $\Pi$ as a (possibly infinite) sequence of alternating nodes and edges $\Pi = n_1 e_1 n_2 \cdots$.

nodes.name: Path projection
nodes.statement: Let $\Pi = n_1 e_1 n_2 \cdots $ be a path of $s$ with respect to $\mathcal{U}$. The \emph{path projection} $\phi(\Pi)$ of $\Pi$ is a sequence of alternating nodes and edges $\phi(\Pi) = \phi(n_1) \phi(e_1) \phi(n_2) \cdots$. Each node $\phi(n)$ is either unlabelled or labelled with a function symbol or variable such that: \begin{enumerate}[(1)] \item if $n$ is labelled $(s, p)$, then $\phi(n)$ is unlabelled if $s|_p$ is a redex in $\mathcal{U}$ or a variable bound by such a redex and it is labelled $\rs{s|_p}$ otherwise, and \item if $n$ is labelled $(r, p, q)$, then $\phi(n)$ is unlabelled if $\rs{r|_p}$ is a meta-variable and it is labelled $\rs{r|_p}$ otherwise. \end{enumerate} Each edge $\phi(e)$ is either labelled with an element of $\mathbb{N}$ or labelled $\epsilon$ such that if $e$ is labelled $i$, then $\phi(e)$ has the same label, and if $e$ is unlabelled, then $\phi(e)$ is labelled $\epsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: The path projection $\phi(\Pi)$ relabels path nodes with function symbols/variables (or unlabelled) and edges with indices or $\epsilon$.

nodes.name: Paths and path projections
nodes.statement: Consider the orthogonal iCRS that only has the following rewrite rule, also denoted $l \rightarrow r$: \[ f([x]Z(x), Z') \rightarrow Z(g(Z(Z'))) \, . \] Given the terms $s = f([x]g(x), a)$ and $t = g(g(g(a)))$ and the set $\mathcal{U}$ containing the only redex in $s$, we have that $s \rightarrow t$ is a complete development of $\mathcal{U}$. The term $s$ has one maximal path with respect to $\mathcal{U}$: \begin{multline*} (s, \epsilon) \rightarrow (r, \epsilon, \epsilon) \rightarrow (s, 10) \overset{1}{\rightarrow} (s, 101) \rightarrow (r, 1, \epsilon) \overset{1}{\rightarrow} (r, 11, \epsilon) \\ \rightarrow (s, 10) \overset{1}{\rightarrow} (s, 101) \rightarrow (r, 111, \epsilon) \rightarrow (s, 2) \end{multline*} Moreover, the term $t$ has one maximal path with respect to $\mathcal{U}/(s \rightarrow t) = \emptyset$: \[ (t, \epsilon) \overset{1}{\rightarrow} (t, 1) \overset{1}{\rightarrow} (t, 11) \overset{1}{\rightarrow} (t, 111) \, . \] The path projections of the maximal paths are, respectively, \[ \cdot \overset{\epsilon}{\rightarrow} \cdot \overset{\epsilon}{\rightarrow} g \overset{1}{\rightarrow} \cdot \overset{\epsilon}{\rightarrow} g \overset{1}{\rightarrow} \cdot \overset{\epsilon}{\rightarrow} g \overset{1}{\rightarrow} \cdot \overset{\epsilon}{\rightarrow} \cdot \overset{\epsilon}{\rightarrow} a \] and \[ g \overset{1}{\rightarrow} g \overset{1}{\rightarrow} g \overset{1}{\rightarrow} a \, . \]
nodes.label: ex:paths

nodes.name: Set of maximal path projections
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{P}(s, \mathcal{U})$ denote the set of path projections of \emph{maximal paths} of $s$ with respect to $\mathcal{U}$.

nodes.name: Path projection is a bijection
nodes.statement: The map $\phi$ defines a bijection between the set of paths and the set of path projections, respectively between maximal paths and the path projections in $\mathcal{P}(s, \mathcal{U})$.
conclusions: The map $\phi$ defines a bijection between the set of paths and the set of path projections, respectively between maximal paths and the path projections in $\mathcal{P}(s, \mathcal{U})$.
nodes.label: prop:phibiject

nodes.name: Path projections across a rewrite step
nodes.statement: Let $u \in \mathcal{U}$ and let $s \rightarrow t$ be the rewrite step contracting $u$. There exists a bijection between $\mathcal{P}(s, \mathcal{U})$ and $\mathcal{P}(t, \mathcal{U}/u)$. Given a path projection $\phi(\Pi) \in \mathcal{P}(s, \mathcal{U})$, its image under the bijection is obtained by deleting finite sequences of unlabelled nodes and $\epsilon$-labelled edges from $\phi(\Pi)$. \qed
assumptions: $u \in \mathcal{U}$
$s \rightarrow t$ be the rewrite step contracting $u$
conclusions: There exists a bijection between $\mathcal{P}(s, \mathcal{U})$ and $\mathcal{P}(t, \mathcal{U}/u)$.
its image under the bijection is obtained by deleting finite sequences of unlabelled nodes and $\epsilon$-labelled edges from $\phi(\Pi)$
nodes.label: unlabeldel

nodes.name: Finite jumps property and matching
nodes.statement: The set $\mathcal{U}$ has the \emph{finite jumps property} if no path projection occurring in $\mathcal{P}(s, \mathcal{U})$ contains an infinite sequence of unlabelled nodes and $\epsilon$-labelled edges. Moreover, a term $t$ \emph{matches} $\mathcal{P}(s, \mathcal{U})$ if, for all $\phi(\Pi) \in \mathcal{P}(s, \mathcal{U})$ and all prefixes of $\phi(\Pi)$ ending in a node $\phi(n)$ labelled $f$, it holds that $\rs{t|_p} = f$, where $p$ is the concatenation of the edge labels in the prefix (starting at the first node of $\phi(\Pi)$ and ending in $\phi(n)$).

nodes.name: Unique matching term
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{U}$ has the finite jumps property, then there exists a unique term, denoted $\mathcal{T}(s, \mathcal{U})$, that matches $\mathcal{P}(s, \mathcal{U})$. \qed
assumptions: $\mathcal{U}$ has the finite jumps property
conclusions: there exists a unique term, denoted $\mathcal{T}(s, \mathcal{U})$, that matches $\mathcal{P}(s, \mathcal{U})$
nodes.label: uniqueterm

nodes.name: Finite Jumps Developments Theorem
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{U}$ has the finite jumps property, then: \begin{enumerate}[\em(1)] \item every complete development of $\mathcal{U}$ ends in $\mathcal{T}(s, \mathcal{U})$, \item for any $p \in \pos{s}$, the set of descendants of $p$ by a complete development of $\mathcal{U}$ is independent of the complete development, \item for any redex $u$ of $s$, the set of residuals of $u$ by a complete development of $\mathcal{U}$ is independent of the complete development, and \item $\mathcal{U}$ has a complete development. \qed \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $\mathcal{U}$ has the finite jumps property
conclusions: every complete development of $\mathcal{U}$ ends in $\mathcal{T}(s, \mathcal{U})$
for any $p \in \pos{s}$, the set of descendants of $p$ by a complete development of $\mathcal{U}$ is independent of the complete development
for any redex $u$ of $s$, the set of residuals of $u$ by a complete development of $\mathcal{U}$ is independent of the complete development
$\mathcal{U}$ has a complete development
nodes.statement_short: With the finite jumps property, complete developments exist, end in $\mathcal{T}(s,\mathcal{U})$, and have development-independent descendants and residuals.
nodes.label: fjdt

nodes.name: Complete development iff finite jumps
nodes.statement: The set $\mathcal{U}$ has a complete development if{f} $\mathcal{U}$ has the finite jumps property. \qed
conclusions: The set $\mathcal{U}$ has a complete development if{f} $\mathcal{U}$ has the finite jumps property.
equivalent_conditions: The set $\mathcal{U}$ has a complete development
nodes.label: compimplfinite

nodes.name: Labelling for descendants
nodes.statement: The proof of Theorem \ref{fjdt}(2) is based on a labelling. In analogy to \cite[Section II.2]{K80}, it presupposes a set of labels $\mathcal{K}$ including a special \emph{empty} label $\varepsilon$. Using the labels, \emph{labelled alternatives} are defined for all function symbols $f$ and variables $x$ and for all labels $k \in \mathcal{K}$, these are denoted $f^k$ and $x^k$, where $f$ and $f^k$ have the same arity. A \emph{labelling} of a (meta-)term replaces each function symbol and variable (including the variables that occur in abstractions) by a labelled alternative, assuming that the labels of variables are ignored where \emph{bindings} and \emph{valuations} are concerned. The labelled version of the assumed orthogonal iCRS includes for every rewrite rule $l \rightarrow r$ and every possible labelling $l'$ of $l$ a rewrite rule $l' \rightarrow r'$, where $r'$ is the labelling of $r$ that labels all function symbols and variables with $\varepsilon$. The labelled version of the iCRS is easily shown to be orthogonal (see \cite[Proposition II.2.6]{K80}). Each reduction in the labelled version corresponds to a reduction in the original iCRS by removal of all labels. Moreover, given a reduction in the original iCRS and a labelling for the initial term, there exists a unique reduction in the labelled version such that removal of the labels gives the reduction we started out with. Finally, given a term in which some subterms are labelled $k$, the descendants of these subterms across some reduction are precisely the subterms labelled $k$ in the final term. These descendants are exactly the descendants obtained in the corresponding unlabelled reduction.
nodes.statement_short: Labelled iCRS versions: labels track descendants exactly, and labelled and unlabelled reductions correspond one-to-one.
nodes.label: rem:label

nodes.name: Fully-extended orthogonal iCRSs throughout
nodes.statement: From this point onwards, we concentrate on the exposition and development of new results, assuming fully-extended, orthogonal iCRSs throughout.

nodes.name: Strip Lemma
nodes.statement: This is effectively an application of the Strip Lemma, which states that a reduction can be projected over a single rewrite step.
conclusions: a reduction can be projected over a single rewrite step

nodes.name: Strip Lemma fails for infinitary higher-order rewriting
nodes.statement: Unfortunately, the Strip Lemma fails in the infinitary higher-order case, as can already be witnessed in i$\lambda$c\xspace \cite{KKSV97,T03_KV}.

nodes.name: Relation to van Oostrom, Sekar-Ramakrishnan and Middeldorp
nodes.statement: As can be inferred from the above, van Oostrom's technique of essential rewrite steps \cite{O99}, as adapted by us, incorporates a proof technique originally developed by Sekar and Ramakrishnan \cite{SR90} to study normalising strategies in first-order rewriting; a technique later refined by Middeldorp \cite{M97}. In fact, van Oostrom's technique can be seen as a higher-order variant of the techniques by Sekar and Ramakrishnan and Middeldorp. Unlike van Oostrom, the latter do not require the introduction of the notion of essentiality, which derives from \cite{K88,GK94}. The filtering described earlier in this section already makes sense in the finite higher-order case, as dealt with by van Oostrom \cite{O99}: It also helps to cope with the nestings that can occur in these systems when defining the appropriate measure. Contrary to all other techniques, which apply only to finite reductions, our instalment revolves around finite sequences of complete developments. As stated previously, the shift to finite sequences is \emph{necessary} in the setting of infinitary rewriting because projecting one reduction step over another may yield an infinite complete development of the residuals of the projected redex.
nodes.statement_short: The adapted essential-steps technique generalises Sekar-Ramakrishnan/Middeldorp; finite sequences of complete developments are needed in the infinitary case.

nodes.name: Prefix set
nodes.statement: A \emph{prefix set} of a term $s$ is a finite set $P \subseteq \pos{s}$ such that all prefixes of positions in $P$ are also in $P$.
differentia: all prefixes of positions in $P$ are also in $P$
also_stated_at: These are \emph{finite} sets of positions such that if a position is included in the set, then all its prefix positions are also included in the set.

nodes.name: Redevelopment of essential rewrite steps
nodes.statement: The material in this section completely redevelops the theory of essential rewrite steps for iCRSs that previously appeared in \cite{JJ05b}. The current theory allows for rewrite rules with infinite right-hand sides, while previously only finite right-hand sides were allowed.

nodes.name: Path prefix set
nodes.statement: Let $s$ and $t$ be terms, $\mathcal{U}$ a set of redexes in $s$ such that $s \Rightarrow^\mathcal{U} t$ and $P$ a prefix set of $t$. The \emph{path prefix set} of $P$ with respect to $\mathcal{U}$ is the set of all paths $\Pi$ of $s$ with respect to $\mathcal{U}$ such that the concatenation of the edge labels of the path projection $\phi(\Pi)$ is in $P$.

nodes.name: Path prefix sets are prefix-closed
nodes.statement: Observe that if a certain path is included in a path prefix set, then all its prefixes are also included in the set.
assumptions: a certain path is included in a path prefix set
conclusions: all its prefixes are also included in the set

nodes.name: Proof that path prefix sets are prefix-closed
nodes.statement: This follows by the dependence on prefix sets and their closure under the prefix relation on positions.
nodes.statement_short: Direct from the prefix closure of prefix sets.

nodes.name: Path prefix set example
nodes.statement: Consider the iCRS from Example \ref{ex:paths}, where $s = f([x]g(x),a)$ and $t = g(g(g(a)))$. The set $P = \{ \epsilon, 1, 11 \}$ is a prefix set of $t$. Let $\mathcal{U}$ be the set containing the only redex of $s$ and observe that $s \Rightarrow^\mathcal{U} t$. The path prefix set of $P$ with respect to $\mathcal{U}$ is the set of all paths that are prefixes of \[ (s,\epsilon) \rightarrow (r,\epsilon,\epsilon) \rightarrow (s,10) \overset{1}{\rightarrow} (s,101) \rightarrow (r,1,\epsilon) \overset{1}{\rightarrow} (r,11,\epsilon) \rightarrow (s,10) \, . \]
nodes.label: ex:path_prefixes

nodes.name: Map zeta
nodes.statement: Let $s$ be a term and $\mathcal{U}$ a set of redexes in $s$. The map $\zeta$ from \emph{finite} paths $\Pi$ of $s$ with respect to $\mathcal{U}$, with final node $n$, to \emph{finite} subsets of $\pos{s}$ is defined as follows: \[ \zeta(\Pi) = \begin{cases} \{ p \} & \text{if $n = (s, p)$ and no redex in $\mathcal{U}$ occurs at $p$} \\ Q & \text{if $n = (s, p)$ and a redex $u \in \mathcal{U}$ occurs at $p$} \\ \emptyset & \text{if $n = (r, p, \redpos{u})$} \end{cases} \] where $Q$ is the set of positions of $s$ that occur in the redex pattern of $u$.
nodes.statement_short: $\zeta$ maps a finite path to its final position, the redex pattern positions of a redex it ends at, or nothing for rhs nodes.

nodes.name: zeta yields a prefix set
nodes.statement: Let $s$ and $t$ be terms, $\mathcal{U}$ a set of redexes in $s$ such that $s \Rightarrow^\mathcal{U} t$, and $P$ a prefix set of $t$. If $\Psi$ is the path prefix set of $P$ with respect to $\mathcal{U}$, then $\zeta(\Psi) = \{ \zeta(\Pi) \; | \; \Pi \in \Psi\}$ is well-defined and yields a prefix set of $s$.
assumptions: $s$ and $t$ be terms, $\mathcal{U}$ a set of redexes in $s$ such that $s \Rightarrow^\mathcal{U} t$, and $P$ a prefix set of $t$
$\Psi$ is the path prefix set of $P$ with respect to $\mathcal{U}$
conclusions: $\zeta(\Psi) = \{ \zeta(\Pi) \; | \; \Pi \in \Psi\}$ is well-defined and yields a prefix set of $s$
nodes.label: lem:zetaprefix

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.6
nodes.statement: \proof Let $\Psi$ be the path prefix set of $P$ with respect to $\mathcal{U}$. Since $\mathcal{U}$ has a complete development, it follows by Lemma \ref{compimplfinite} that $\mathcal{U}$ has the finite jumps property, i.e.\ all path projections in $\mathcal{P}(s, \mathcal{U})$ contain only finite sequences of unlabelled nodes and $\epsilon$-labelled edges. As each path is a prefix of a maximal path, whose path projections are in $\mathcal{P}(s, \mathcal{U})$, it follows by definition of path projections and the finite jumps property that each path in $\Psi$ is finite. Hence, $\zeta(\Psi)$ is well-defined. This leaves to show that $\zeta(\Psi)$ yields a prefix set of $s$, i.e.\ that $\zeta(\Psi)$ is finite and that each prefix of a position in $\zeta(\Psi)$ is also in $\zeta(\Psi)$. For each position in the prefix set $P$ of $t$ a finite number of paths is included in $\Psi$. This follows by induction on the length of the positions, employing the fact that $\mathcal{U}$ has the finite jumps property and the fact that the extension of a path is uniquely determined by the definition of paths and the considered position. Since $P$ is finite, the same now follows for $\Psi$. Hence, as $\zeta$ maps each finite path to a finite number of positions, $\zeta(\Psi)$ is finite. Let $p \in \zeta(\Psi)$ and $q < p$. There are two possibilities: $q$ occurs either in the redex pattern of a redex in $\mathcal{U}$, or not. In case $q$ occurs in the redex pattern of a redex $u \in \mathcal{U}$, it follows by $p \in \zeta(\Psi)$ and the definition of paths that there exists a path in the path prefix set which ends in the node $(s, \redpos{u})$, with $\redpos{u}$ the position of the redex $u$. Hence, in this case $q \in \zeta(\Psi)$ by definition of $\zeta$. In case $q$ does not occur in a redex pattern, it follows by the definition of paths and the inclusion of $p$ in $\zeta(\Psi)$ that there exists a path in the path prefix set which ends in the node $(s, q)$ and, thus, $q \in \zeta(\Psi)$. Hence, all prefixes of positions in $\zeta(\Psi)$ are included in $\zeta(\Psi)$. Employing the finiteness of $\zeta(\Psi)$ it now follows that $\zeta(\Psi)$ yields a prefix of $s$, as required. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Finite jumps property makes all paths in $\Psi$ finite; induction on position length gives finiteness, and a case split gives prefix closure.

nodes.name: Finite jumps property
nodes.statement: Let $\Psi$ be the path prefix set of $P$ with respect to $\mathcal{U}$. Since $\mathcal{U}$ has a complete development, it follows by Lemma \ref{compimplfinite} that $\mathcal{U}$ has the finite jumps property, i.e.\ all path projections in $\mathcal{P}(s, \mathcal{U})$ contain only finite sequences of unlabelled nodes and $\epsilon$-labelled edges.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $\Psi$; by Lemma 2.36 $\mathcal{U}$ has the finite jumps property.

nodes.name: Well-definedness
nodes.statement: As each path is a prefix of a maximal path, whose path projections are in $\mathcal{P}(s, \mathcal{U})$, it follows by definition of path projections and the finite jumps property that each path in $\Psi$ is finite. Hence, $\zeta(\Psi)$ is well-defined.
nodes.statement_short: Every path in $\Psi$ is finite, so $\zeta(\Psi)$ is well-defined.

nodes.name: Remaining obligations
nodes.statement: This leaves to show that $\zeta(\Psi)$ yields a prefix set of $s$, i.e.\ that $\zeta(\Psi)$ is finite and that each prefix of a position in $\zeta(\Psi)$ is also in $\zeta(\Psi)$.
nodes.statement_short: Remains: finiteness and prefix closure.

nodes.name: Finiteness
nodes.statement: For each position in the prefix set $P$ of $t$ a finite number of paths is included in $\Psi$. This follows by induction on the length of the positions, employing the fact that $\mathcal{U}$ has the finite jumps property and the fact that the extension of a path is uniquely determined by the definition of paths and the considered position. Since $P$ is finite, the same now follows for $\Psi$. Hence, as $\zeta$ maps each finite path to a finite number of positions, $\zeta(\Psi)$ is finite.
nodes.statement_short: By induction on position length, finitely many paths per position, so $\zeta(\Psi)$ is finite.

nodes.name: Prefix closure
nodes.statement: Let $p \in \zeta(\Psi)$ and $q < p$. There are two possibilities: $q$ occurs either in the redex pattern of a redex in $\mathcal{U}$, or not. In case $q$ occurs in the redex pattern of a redex $u \in \mathcal{U}$, it follows by $p \in \zeta(\Psi)$ and the definition of paths that there exists a path in the path prefix set which ends in the node $(s, \redpos{u})$, with $\redpos{u}$ the position of the redex $u$. Hence, in this case $q \in \zeta(\Psi)$ by definition of $\zeta$. In case $q$ does not occur in a redex pattern, it follows by the definition of paths and the inclusion of $p$ in $\zeta(\Psi)$ that there exists a path in the path prefix set which ends in the node $(s, q)$ and, thus, $q \in \zeta(\Psi)$. Hence, all prefixes of positions in $\zeta(\Psi)$ are included in $\zeta(\Psi)$. Employing the finiteness of $\zeta(\Psi)$ it now follows that $\zeta(\Psi)$ yields a prefix of $s$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: Case split on whether a prefix $q$ lies in a redex pattern shows prefix closure.

nodes.name: Take prefix
nodes.statement: Let $p \in \zeta(\Psi)$ and $q < p$. There are two possibilities: $q$ occurs either in the redex pattern of a redex in $\mathcal{U}$, or not.
nodes.statement_short: Take $q < p$ and split on redex-pattern membership.

nodes.name: Case: in redex pattern
nodes.statement: In case $q$ occurs in the redex pattern of a redex $u \in \mathcal{U}$, it follows by $p \in \zeta(\Psi)$ and the definition of paths that there exists a path in the path prefix set which ends in the node $(s, \redpos{u})$, with $\redpos{u}$ the position of the redex $u$. Hence, in this case $q \in \zeta(\Psi)$ by definition of $\zeta$.
nodes.statement_short: A path ending at the redex node puts $q$ in $\zeta(\Psi)$.

nodes.name: Case: not in redex pattern
nodes.statement: In case $q$ does not occur in a redex pattern, it follows by the definition of paths and the inclusion of $p$ in $\zeta(\Psi)$ that there exists a path in the path prefix set which ends in the node $(s, q)$ and, thus, $q \in \zeta(\Psi)$.
nodes.statement_short: A path ending at $(s,q)$ puts $q$ in $\zeta(\Psi)$.

nodes.name: Conclude prefix set
nodes.statement: Hence, all prefixes of positions in $\zeta(\Psi)$ are included in $\zeta(\Psi)$. Employing the finiteness of $\zeta(\Psi)$ it now follows that $\zeta(\Psi)$ yields a prefix of $s$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: Prefix closure plus finiteness gives a prefix set.

nodes.name: Map epsilon (propagation of prefix sets)
nodes.statement: Let $s$ and $t$ be terms and $\mathcal{U}$ a set of redexes in $s$ such that $s \Rightarrow^\mathcal{U} t$. The map $\varepsilon$ from prefix sets $P$ of $t$ to prefix sets of $s$ is defined as: \[ \pmapp{P}{s \Rightarrow^\mathcal{U} t} = \zeta(\Psi) \] where $\Psi$ is the path prefix set of $P$ with respect to $\mathcal{U}$.
also_stated_at: The map is first defined on complete developments $s \Rightarrow^\mathcal{U} t$: Given a prefix set $P$ of $t$ the map yields a prefix set of $s$, which we denote by $\pmapp{P}{s \Rightarrow^\mathcal{U} t}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\varepsilon$ maps a prefix set $P$ of $t$ to $\zeta$ of its path prefix set, a prefix set of $s$.
nodes.label: def:pmap

nodes.name: Essential and inessential positions and redexes
nodes.statement: Let $s$ and $t$ be terms, $\mathcal{U}$ a set of redexes in $s$ such that $s \Rightarrow^\mathcal{U} t$, and $P$ a prefix set of $t$. A position $p$ of $s$, respectively a redex $u$ in $s$, is called \emph{essential} for $P$ if $p$, respectively the position of $u$, occurs in $\pmapp{P}{s \Rightarrow^\mathcal{U} t}$. A position, respectively a redex, is called \emph{inessential} otherwise.
also_stated_at: Moreover, we call a position $p$ of $s$, respectively a redex $u$ in $s$, \emph{essential} if $p$, respectively the position of $u$, occurs in $\pmapp{P}{s \Rightarrow^\mathcal{U} t}$. They are called \emph{inessential} otherwise.
nodes.label: def:essential

nodes.name: Essential positions example
nodes.statement: Consider the prefix set $P$ in Example \ref{ex:path_prefixes}. We have that the positions $\epsilon$, $1$, $10$, and $101$ are essential for $P$ in $s$.

nodes.name: Extension of epsilon to finite sequences of complete developments
nodes.statement: As the set of positions obtained through application of $\varepsilon$ is a prefix set, the map is easily extended to a finite sequence of complete developments $s_0 \Rightarrow^{\mathcal{U}_1} s_1 \Rightarrow^{\mathcal{U}_2} \cdots \Rightarrow^{\mathcal{U}_n} s_n$: In case of $s_n$, define $\pmaph{P}$ to be $P$. In case of $s_i$, with $i < n$, define $\pmaph{P}$ to be $\pmapp{P_{i + 1}}{s_i \Rightarrow^{\mathcal{U}_{i + 1}} s_{i + 1}}$ where $P_{i + 1}$ is the prefix set obtained for $s_{i + 1}$. The notion of (in)essentiality is extended accordingly.
nodes.statement_short: $\varepsilon$ is extended backwards along a finite sequence of complete developments by iterating it development by development.

nodes.name: Essential positions descend into the prefix set
nodes.statement: Let $s$ and $t$ be terms, $\mathcal{U}$ a set of redexes in $s$ such that $s \Rightarrow^\mathcal{U} t$, and $P$ a prefix set of $t$. If $p \in \pos{s}$ does not occur in the redex pattern of a redex in $\mathcal{U}$ and is not the position of a variable bound by a redex in $\mathcal{U}$, then $p$ is essential if{f} there exists a position $q \in P$ such that $q \in p/(s \Rightarrow t)$ and $p$ is inessential if{f} no descendant of $p$ occurs in~$P$.
assumptions: $s$ and $t$ be terms, $\mathcal{U}$ a set of redexes in $s$ such that $s \Rightarrow^\mathcal{U} t$, and $P$ a prefix set of $t$
$p \in \pos{s}$ does not occur in the redex pattern of a redex in $\mathcal{U}$ and is not the position of a variable bound by a redex in $\mathcal{U}$
conclusions: $p$ is essential if{f} there exists a position $q \in P$ such that $q \in p/(s \Rightarrow t)$
$p$ is inessential if{f} no descendant of $p$ occurs in~$P$
equivalent_conditions: there exists a position $q \in P$ such that $q \in p/(s \Rightarrow t)$
nodes.statement_short: Outside redex patterns, a position is essential iff it has a descendant in $P$.
nodes.label: prop:desess

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.10
nodes.statement: \proof By Lemma \ref{compimplfinite}, it follows that $\mathcal{U}$ has the finite jumps property. Employing the labelling from the proof of Theorem \ref{fjdt}(2) and its properties relating labelled and unlabelled reductions and descendants across these reductions --- as exhibited in Remark \ref{rem:label} --- together with Theorem \ref{fjdt}(1), it is easy to see that a position $p \in \pos{s}$ descends to a position $q \in \pos{t}$ if{f} $p$ does not occur in a redex pattern of a redex in $\mathcal{U}$ and there exists a finite path $\Pi$ with final node $n = (s, p)$ such that $\phi(n)$ is labelled and such that the concatenation of the edge labels of the path projection of $\Pi$ is $q$. Since $\zeta(\Pi) = \{ p \}$, the result follows by definition of path prefix sets. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Via the labelling of Remark 2.37 and the Finite Jumps Developments Theorem, descendants correspond to finite paths ending at $(s,p)$.

nodes.name: Finite jumps
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{compimplfinite}, it follows that $\mathcal{U}$ has the finite jumps property.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.36 gives the finite jumps property.

nodes.name: Characterise descendants by paths
nodes.statement: Employing the labelling from the proof of Theorem \ref{fjdt}(2) and its properties relating labelled and unlabelled reductions and descendants across these reductions --- as exhibited in Remark \ref{rem:label} --- together with Theorem \ref{fjdt}(1), it is easy to see that a position $p \in \pos{s}$ descends to a position $q \in \pos{t}$ if{f} $p$ does not occur in a redex pattern of a redex in $\mathcal{U}$ and there exists a finite path $\Pi$ with final node $n = (s, p)$ such that $\phi(n)$ is labelled and such that the concatenation of the edge labels of the path projection of $\Pi$ is $q$.
nodes.statement_short: Labelling and Theorem 2.35(1) characterise descendants by finite paths.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since $\zeta(\Pi) = \{ p \}$, the result follows by definition of path prefix sets.
nodes.statement_short: Since $\zeta(\Pi)=\{p\}$ the result follows.

nodes.name: Finite sequence of complete developments notation
nodes.statement: By $D$, respectively $E$, we denote a finite sequence of complete developments $\fscd{s}{U}{n}$, respectively $\fscd{t}{V}{n}$, of length $n$. Moreover, if $P$ is a prefix set of $s_n$, then for all $0 \leq i \leq n$ we denote by $P_i$ the set of positions essential for $P$ in $s_i$.

nodes.name: Measure
nodes.statement: The \emph{measure} $\pmep{P}{D}$ of $D$ with respect to the prefix set $P$ of $s_n$ is the $n$-tuple $(l_n,\ldots,l_1)$ --- note the reverse order! --- such that $l_i$, with $1 \leq i \leq n$, is the cardinality of the path prefix set of $P_i$ with respect to $\mathcal{U}_i$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mu_P(D)$ is the reversed tuple of the sizes of the path prefix sets of the essential positions along $D$.
nodes.label: measuredef

nodes.name: Well-founded order on measures
nodes.statement: As already mentioned, the tuples in the above definition are compared first length-wise and next lexicographically (in the natural order). This yields a well-founded order, as each element of a tuple is finite by Lemma \ref{lem:zetaprefix}. We denote this order by $\prec$.
also_stated_at: Tuples are compared first length-wise and next lexicographically (in the natural order). This yields a well-founded order --- as the natural order on natural numbers is well-founded --- which we denote by $\prec$.

nodes.name: Mirroring
nodes.statement: Let $s$ and $t$ be terms and $P$ a prefix set of $s$. The term $t$ \emph{mirrors} $s$ in $P$, if $P \subseteq \pos{t}$ and $\rs{t|_p} = \rs{s|_p}$ for all $p \in P$. Let $P$ be a prefix set of $s_n$ in $D$. The finite sequence $E$ \emph{mirrors} $D$ in $P$ if for all $0 \leq i \leq n$ it holds that the set of positions essential for $P$ in $t_i$ is $P_i$, $t_i$ mirrors $s_i$ in $P_i$, and the path prefix set of $P_i$ with respect to $\mathcal{V}_i$ is identical to the path prefix set of $P_i$ with respect to $\mathcal{U}_i$.
nodes.statement_short: $t$ mirrors $s$ in $P$ if root symbols agree on $P$; sequences mirror if essential sets, root symbols and path prefix sets agree stepwise.

nodes.name: Cut-down to finite essential developments
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a prefix set of $s_n$ in $D$ and let $t_0$ mirror $s_0$ in the positions essential for $P$ in $s_0$. There exists a finite sequence $E$, with $\mathcal{V}_i$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n$ \emph{finite} and consisting \emph{solely} of essential redexes, such that $E$ mirrors $D$ in $P$ and $\pmep{P}{E} = \pmep{P}{D}$.
assumptions: $P$ be a prefix set of $s_n$ in $D$
$t_0$ mirror $s_0$ in the positions essential for $P$ in $s_0$
conclusions: There exists a finite sequence $E$, with $\mathcal{V}_i$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n$ \emph{finite} and consisting \emph{solely} of essential redexes, such that $E$ mirrors $D$ in $P$ and $\pmep{P}{E} = \pmep{P}{D}$
nodes.statement_short: A sequence of complete developments can be cut down to finite sets of essential redexes, preserving mirroring and the measure.
nodes.label: lem:simple_proj

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.14
nodes.statement: \proof By induction on $n$, the number of complete developments in $D$. In case $n = 0$, the result is immediate by definition of $t_0$. In case $n > 0$, let $\mathcal{U}'_n$ contain the redexes from $\mathcal{U}_n$ essential for $P$. Observe for each $u \in \mathcal{U}'_n$ that all positions in the redex pattern of $u$ occur at positions in $P_{n - 1}$ by definition of the map $\zeta$. Hence, since we have by the induction hypothesis that $t_{n - 1}$ mirrors $s_{n - 1}$ in $P_{n - 1}$, it follows by orthogonality and fully-extendedness that there exists for each redex in $\mathcal{U}'_n$ a redex in $t_{n - 1}$ at the same position and employing the same rewrite rule. Define $\mathcal{V}_n$ to be the set of these corresponding redexes in $t_{n - 1}$. Obviously, the sets $\mathcal{V}_n$ and $\mathcal{U}'_n$ have the same cardinality, which is finite as $P_{n - 1}$ is finite. Since $\mathcal{V}_n$ is finite, it follows by Lemma \ref{lem:finite_dev} that there exists a complete development $t_{n-1} \Rightarrow^{\mathcal{V}_n} t_n$. Moreover, since $P_{n - 1}$ is a prefix set and $t_{n - 1}$ mirrors $s_{n - 1}$ in $P_{n - 1}$, it follows by definition of paths and $\mathcal{V}_n$ that for each path of $s_{n - 1}$ with respect to $\mathcal{U}_n$ occurring in the path prefix set of $P$ there exists an identical path of $t_{n - 1}$ with respect to $\mathcal{V}_n$. Hence, by definition of path projections, we have for the terms matching $\mathcal{P}(s_{n - 1}, \mathcal{U}_n)$ and $\mathcal{P}(t_{n - 1}, \mathcal{V}_n)$, i.e.\ $s_n$ and $t_n$, that $P \subseteq \pos{t_n}$, $\rs{s_n|_p} = \rs{t_n|_p}$ for all $p \in P$, and that all positions in $P_{n - 1}$ and redexes in $\mathcal{V}_n$ are essential for $P$. The induction hypothesis now furnishes the result. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the number $n$ of developments. The step keeps only essential redexes of $\mathcal{U}_n$, finite by $\zeta$, and develops them by Lemma 2.26.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: By induction on $n$, the number of complete developments in $D$. In case $n = 0$, the result is immediate by definition of $t_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$; $n=0$ is immediate.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: In case $n > 0$, let $\mathcal{U}'_n$ contain the redexes from $\mathcal{U}_n$ essential for $P$. Observe for each $u \in \mathcal{U}'_n$ that all positions in the redex pattern of $u$ occur at positions in $P_{n - 1}$ by definition of the map $\zeta$. Hence, since we have by the induction hypothesis that $t_{n - 1}$ mirrors $s_{n - 1}$ in $P_{n - 1}$, it follows by orthogonality and fully-extendedness that there exists for each redex in $\mathcal{U}'_n$ a redex in $t_{n - 1}$ at the same position and employing the same rewrite rule. Define $\mathcal{V}_n$ to be the set of these corresponding redexes in $t_{n - 1}$. Obviously, the sets $\mathcal{V}_n$ and $\mathcal{U}'_n$ have the same cardinality, which is finite as $P_{n - 1}$ is finite. Since $\mathcal{V}_n$ is finite, it follows by Lemma \ref{lem:finite_dev} that there exists a complete development $t_{n-1} \Rightarrow^{\mathcal{V}_n} t_n$. Moreover, since $P_{n - 1}$ is a prefix set and $t_{n - 1}$ mirrors $s_{n - 1}$ in $P_{n - 1}$, it follows by definition of paths and $\mathcal{V}_n$ that for each path of $s_{n - 1}$ with respect to $\mathcal{U}_n$ occurring in the path prefix set of $P$ there exists an identical path of $t_{n - 1}$ with respect to $\mathcal{V}_n$. Hence, by definition of path projections, we have for the terms matching $\mathcal{P}(s_{n - 1}, \mathcal{U}_n)$ and $\mathcal{P}(t_{n - 1}, \mathcal{V}_n)$, i.e.\ $s_n$ and $t_n$, that $P \subseteq \pos{t_n}$, $\rs{s_n|_p} = \rs{t_n|_p}$ for all $p \in P$, and that all positions in $P_{n - 1}$ and redexes in $\mathcal{V}_n$ are essential for $P$. The induction hypothesis now furnishes the result.
nodes.statement_short: Construct $\mathcal{V}_n$ from the essential redexes and verify mirroring.

nodes.name: Essential redexes
nodes.statement: In case $n > 0$, let $\mathcal{U}'_n$ contain the redexes from $\mathcal{U}_n$ essential for $P$. Observe for each $u \in \mathcal{U}'_n$ that all positions in the redex pattern of $u$ occur at positions in $P_{n - 1}$ by definition of the map $\zeta$.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to the essential redexes $\mathcal{U}'_n$, whose patterns lie in $P_{n-1}$.

nodes.name: Corresponding redexes
nodes.statement: Hence, since we have by the induction hypothesis that $t_{n - 1}$ mirrors $s_{n - 1}$ in $P_{n - 1}$, it follows by orthogonality and fully-extendedness that there exists for each redex in $\mathcal{U}'_n$ a redex in $t_{n - 1}$ at the same position and employing the same rewrite rule.
nodes.statement_short: By IH, orthogonality and fully-extendedness, matching redexes exist in $t_{n-1}$.

nodes.name: Define V_n
nodes.statement: Define $\mathcal{V}_n$ to be the set of these corresponding redexes in $t_{n - 1}$. Obviously, the sets $\mathcal{V}_n$ and $\mathcal{U}'_n$ have the same cardinality, which is finite as $P_{n - 1}$ is finite.
nodes.statement_short: Define the finite set $\mathcal{V}_n$.

nodes.name: Finite complete development
nodes.statement: Since $\mathcal{V}_n$ is finite, it follows by Lemma \ref{lem:finite_dev} that there exists a complete development $t_{n-1} \Rightarrow^{\mathcal{V}_n} t_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.26 gives a complete development of $\mathcal{V}_n$.

nodes.name: Identical paths
nodes.statement: Moreover, since $P_{n - 1}$ is a prefix set and $t_{n - 1}$ mirrors $s_{n - 1}$ in $P_{n - 1}$, it follows by definition of paths and $\mathcal{V}_n$ that for each path of $s_{n - 1}$ with respect to $\mathcal{U}_n$ occurring in the path prefix set of $P$ there exists an identical path of $t_{n - 1}$ with respect to $\mathcal{V}_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Paths in the path prefix set coincide in $s_{n-1}$ and $t_{n-1}$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence, by definition of path projections, we have for the terms matching $\mathcal{P}(s_{n - 1}, \mathcal{U}_n)$ and $\mathcal{P}(t_{n - 1}, \mathcal{V}_n)$, i.e.\ $s_n$ and $t_n$, that $P \subseteq \pos{t_n}$, $\rs{s_n|_p} = \rs{t_n|_p}$ for all $p \in P$, and that all positions in $P_{n - 1}$ and redexes in $\mathcal{V}_n$ are essential for $P$. The induction hypothesis now furnishes the result.
nodes.statement_short: Final terms agree on $P$; the IH gives the result.

nodes.name: Emaciated projection across a step
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a prefix set of $s_n$ in $D$. If $s_0 \rightarrow t_0$ contracts a redex $u$ such that no redex in $u/D$ occurs at a position in $P$, then the \emph{emaciated projection} of $D$ across $s_0 \rightarrow t_0$ with respect to $P$, written $D \mathord{\sslash} u$, is defined as $E/u$, where $E$ is the result of applying Lemma \ref{lem:simple_proj} to $D$ with $E$ starting in $s_0$.
nodes.statement_short: $D \sslash u$: cut $D$ down by Lemma 4.14, then project it over $u$, provided no residual of $u$ lands in $P$.
nodes.label: def:emmy

nodes.name: Existence and mirroring of the emaciated projection
nodes.statement: That the projection $E/u$ in the above definition exists follows by repeated application of Proposition \ref{prop:finite_over_normal}. The proposition can be applied since each set of redexes developed along $E$ is finite. Since $E$ mirrors $D$ in $P$, orthogonality and fully-extendedness imply that no redex in $u/E$ occurs at a position in $P$ and, hence, the final term of $E/u$ mirrors the final one of $D$ in $P$. Moreover, in case $u$ is inessential, the requirement that no redex in $u/D$ occurs at a position in $P$ is void by Proposition \ref{prop:desess}. If such a redex would occur, it would be essential.
nodes.statement_short: $E/u$ exists by Proposition 2.27; its final term mirrors that of $D$ in $P$, and for inessential $u$ the side condition is automatic.

nodes.name: Projection over an essential step decreases the measure
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a prefix set of $s_n$ in $D$. If $s_0 \rightarrow t_0$ contracts an essential redex $u$ such that no redex in $u/D$ occurs at a position in $P$, then $\pmep{P}{D \mathord{\sslash} u} \prec \pmep{P}{D}$.
assumptions: $P$ be a prefix set of $s_n$ in $D$
$s_0 \rightarrow t_0$ contracts an essential redex $u$ such that no redex in $u/D$ occurs at a position in $P$
conclusions: $\pmep{P}{D \mathord{\sslash} u} \prec \pmep{P}{D}$
nodes.label: lem:essential_then_decrease

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.16
nodes.statement: \proof Suppose that $s_0 \rightarrow t_0$ contracts an essential redex $u$ such that no redex in $u/D$ occurs at a position in $P$. Denote by $E$ the result of applying Lemma \ref{lem:simple_proj} to $D$, with $E$ starting in $s_0$, and write $E/u$ as $\fscdp{t}{V}{n}$ where $\mathcal{V}'_i = \mathcal{V}_i / (t_{i - 1} \Rightarrow t'_{i - 1})$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n$. Let $i < n$ be the largest index of a set $\mathcal{U}_i$ that contains a residual of $u$ that is essential. Since $E$ mirrors $D$ in $P$, the index $i$ is also the largest index of a set $\mathcal{V}_i$ that contains a residual of $u$ that is essential. No residual of $u$ occurs at an essential position in $t_j$ for $i < j \leq n$. Otherwise, a residual also occurs at an essential position in $t_{j + 1}$ by definition of residuals and Proposition \ref{prop:desess}. Iteratively, a residual then occurs in $t_n$ at a position in $P$, contradicting assumptions. Hence, by induction we have for all $i < j \leq n$ that $t'_j$ mirrors $t_j$ in $P_j$, where $P_j$ is the set of positions essential for $P$ in both $t'_j$ and $t_j$. Moreover, for each essential redex in $\mathcal{V}'_j$ there exists an essential redex in $\mathcal{V}_j$ at the same position and employing the same rewrite rule, and vice versa. Write $\pmep{P}{E} = (l_n, \ldots, l_1)$ and $\pmep{P}{E/u} = (l'_n,\ldots,l'_1)$. For all $j < i$, the cardinality of the path prefix set of $\mathcal{V}'_j$ may be different from the one of $\mathcal{V}_j$, i.e.\ we may have $l'_j \not = l_j$. The cardinality of the path prefix set of $\mathcal{V}'_i$ is less than that of $\mathcal{V}_i$ by Proposition \ref{prop:phibiject} and Lemma \ref{unlabeldel}. Hence, $l'_i < l_i$. Finally, for all $i < k \leq n$ the path prefix sets of $\mathcal{V}'_k$ and $\mathcal{V}_k$ have the same cardinality by the correspondence between the essential redexes, i.e.\ $l'_k = l_k$. Thus, $\pmep{P}{E/u} \prec \pmep{P}{E}$. By Lemma \ref{lem:simple_proj} it now follows that $\pmep{P}{D \mathord{\sslash} u} \prec \pmep{P}{D}$, as required. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Take the largest index with an essential residual of $u$; the measure strictly drops there (Prop. 2.31, Lemma 2.32) and is unchanged above.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Suppose that $s_0 \rightarrow t_0$ contracts an essential redex $u$ such that no redex in $u/D$ occurs at a position in $P$. Denote by $E$ the result of applying Lemma \ref{lem:simple_proj} to $D$, with $E$ starting in $s_0$, and write $E/u$ as $\fscdp{t}{V}{n}$ where $\mathcal{V}'_i = \mathcal{V}_i / (t_{i - 1} \Rightarrow t'_{i - 1})$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume the hypotheses and write $E/u$ for the cut-down projection.

nodes.name: Largest essential index
nodes.statement: Let $i < n$ be the largest index of a set $\mathcal{U}_i$ that contains a residual of $u$ that is essential. Since $E$ mirrors $D$ in $P$, the index $i$ is also the largest index of a set $\mathcal{V}_i$ that contains a residual of $u$ that is essential. No residual of $u$ occurs at an essential position in $t_j$ for $i < j \leq n$. Otherwise, a residual also occurs at an essential position in $t_{j + 1}$ by definition of residuals and Proposition \ref{prop:desess}. Iteratively, a residual then occurs in $t_n$ at a position in $P$, contradicting assumptions. Hence, by induction we have for all $i < j \leq n$ that $t'_j$ mirrors $t_j$ in $P_j$, where $P_j$ is the set of positions essential for $P$ in both $t'_j$ and $t_j$. Moreover, for each essential redex in $\mathcal{V}'_j$ there exists an essential redex in $\mathcal{V}_j$ at the same position and employing the same rewrite rule, and vice versa.
nodes.statement_short: Above index $i$ the projected sequence mirrors the original.

nodes.name: Choose i
nodes.statement: Let $i < n$ be the largest index of a set $\mathcal{U}_i$ that contains a residual of $u$ that is essential. Since $E$ mirrors $D$ in $P$, the index $i$ is also the largest index of a set $\mathcal{V}_i$ that contains a residual of $u$ that is essential.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $i$ maximal with an essential residual of $u$.

nodes.name: No essential residual above i
nodes.statement: No residual of $u$ occurs at an essential position in $t_j$ for $i < j \leq n$. Otherwise, a residual also occurs at an essential position in $t_{j + 1}$ by definition of residuals and Proposition \ref{prop:desess}. Iteratively, a residual then occurs in $t_n$ at a position in $P$, contradicting assumptions.
nodes.statement_short: An essential residual above $i$ would reach $P$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Mirroring above i
nodes.statement: Hence, by induction we have for all $i < j \leq n$ that $t'_j$ mirrors $t_j$ in $P_j$, where $P_j$ is the set of positions essential for $P$ in both $t'_j$ and $t_j$. Moreover, for each essential redex in $\mathcal{V}'_j$ there exists an essential redex in $\mathcal{V}_j$ at the same position and employing the same rewrite rule, and vice versa.
nodes.statement_short: By induction, mirroring and redex correspondence hold above $i$.

nodes.name: Compare measures
nodes.statement: Write $\pmep{P}{E} = (l_n, \ldots, l_1)$ and $\pmep{P}{E/u} = (l'_n,\ldots,l'_1)$. For all $j < i$, the cardinality of the path prefix set of $\mathcal{V}'_j$ may be different from the one of $\mathcal{V}_j$, i.e.\ we may have $l'_j \not = l_j$. The cardinality of the path prefix set of $\mathcal{V}'_i$ is less than that of $\mathcal{V}_i$ by Proposition \ref{prop:phibiject} and Lemma \ref{unlabeldel}. Hence, $l'_i < l_i$. Finally, for all $i < k \leq n$ the path prefix sets of $\mathcal{V}'_k$ and $\mathcal{V}_k$ have the same cardinality by the correspondence between the essential redexes, i.e.\ $l'_k = l_k$. Thus, $\pmep{P}{E/u} \prec \pmep{P}{E}$. By Lemma \ref{lem:simple_proj} it now follows that $\pmep{P}{D \mathord{\sslash} u} \prec \pmep{P}{D}$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: The tuples agree above $i$ and drop at $i$, so the measure decreases.

nodes.name: Write measures
nodes.statement: Write $\pmep{P}{E} = (l_n, \ldots, l_1)$ and $\pmep{P}{E/u} = (l'_n,\ldots,l'_1)$. For all $j < i$, the cardinality of the path prefix set of $\mathcal{V}'_j$ may be different from the one of $\mathcal{V}_j$, i.e.\ we may have $l'_j \not = l_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Write the two measures; entries below $i$ may differ.

nodes.name: Strict drop at i
nodes.statement: The cardinality of the path prefix set of $\mathcal{V}'_i$ is less than that of $\mathcal{V}_i$ by Proposition \ref{prop:phibiject} and Lemma \ref{unlabeldel}. Hence, $l'_i < l_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 2.31 and Lemma 2.32 give $l'_i < l_i$.

nodes.name: Equal above i
nodes.statement: Finally, for all $i < k \leq n$ the path prefix sets of $\mathcal{V}'_k$ and $\mathcal{V}_k$ have the same cardinality by the correspondence between the essential redexes, i.e.\ $l'_k = l_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Entries above $i$ coincide.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus, $\pmep{P}{E/u} \prec \pmep{P}{E}$. By Lemma \ref{lem:simple_proj} it now follows that $\pmep{P}{D \mathord{\sslash} u} \prec \pmep{P}{D}$, as required.
nodes.statement_short: Hence the measure decreases; transfer to $D$ by Lemma 4.14.

nodes.name: Projection over an inessential step preserves the measure
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a prefix set of $s_n$ in $D$. If $s_0 \rightarrow t_0$ contracts an inessential redex $u$, then $D \mathord{\sslash} u$ mirrors $D$ in $P$ and $\pmep{P}{D \mathord{\sslash} u} = \pmep{P}{D}$.
assumptions: $P$ be a prefix set of $s_n$ in $D$
$s_0 \rightarrow t_0$ contracts an inessential redex $u$
conclusions: $D \mathord{\sslash} u$ mirrors $D$ in $P$
$\pmep{P}{D \mathord{\sslash} u} = \pmep{P}{D}$
nodes.label: lem:inessential_nonroot_then_equal

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.17
nodes.statement: \proof Suppose that $s_0 \rightarrow t_0$ contracts an inessential redex $u$. Denote by $E$ the result of applying Lemma \ref{lem:simple_proj} to $D$, with $E$ starting in $s_0$, and write $E/u$ as $\fscdp{t}{V}{n}$ where $\mathcal{V}'_i = \mathcal{V}_i / (t_{i - 1} \Rightarrow t'_{i - 1})$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n$. For all $0 \leq i < n$, no residual of $u$ occurs at an essential position in $t_i$. Otherwise, as $E$ mirrors $D$ in $P$, it follows that $u$ is essential by repeated application of Proposition \ref{prop:desess}. Hence, by induction we have for all $1 \leq j \leq n$ that $t'_j$ mirrors $t_j$ in $P_j$, where $P_j$ is the set of position essential for $P$ in both $t'_j$ and $t_j$. Moreover, for each essential redex in $\mathcal{V}'_j$ there exists an essential redex in $\mathcal{V}_j$ at the same position and employing the same rewrite rule, and vice versa. For all $1 \leq j \leq n$ the path prefix sets of $\mathcal{V}'_j$ and $\mathcal{V}_j$ are identical by the correspondence between the prefix sets and the essential redexes. Thus, $E/u$ mirrors $E$ in $P$ and $\pmep{P}{E/u} = \pmep{P}{E}$. By Lemma \ref{lem:simple_proj} it now follows that $D \mathord{\sslash} u$ mirrors $D$ in $P$ and that $\pmep{P}{D \mathord{\sslash} u} = \pmep{P}{D}$, as required. \qed
nodes.statement_short: No residual of an inessential $u$ is essential, so by induction the projection mirrors the sequence and path prefix sets coincide.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Suppose that $s_0 \rightarrow t_0$ contracts an inessential redex $u$. Denote by $E$ the result of applying Lemma \ref{lem:simple_proj} to $D$, with $E$ starting in $s_0$, and write $E/u$ as $\fscdp{t}{V}{n}$ where $\mathcal{V}'_i = \mathcal{V}_i / (t_{i - 1} \Rightarrow t'_{i - 1})$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $u$ inessential and write $E/u$.

nodes.name: No essential residuals
nodes.statement: For all $0 \leq i < n$, no residual of $u$ occurs at an essential position in $t_i$. Otherwise, as $E$ mirrors $D$ in $P$, it follows that $u$ is essential by repeated application of Proposition \ref{prop:desess}. Hence, by induction we have for all $1 \leq j \leq n$ that $t'_j$ mirrors $t_j$ in $P_j$, where $P_j$ is the set of position essential for $P$ in both $t'_j$ and $t_j$. Moreover, for each essential redex in $\mathcal{V}'_j$ there exists an essential redex in $\mathcal{V}_j$ at the same position and employing the same rewrite rule, and vice versa.
nodes.statement_short: Residuals of $u$ are never essential (Prop. 4.10), so mirroring propagates by induction.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: For all $1 \leq j \leq n$ the path prefix sets of $\mathcal{V}'_j$ and $\mathcal{V}_j$ are identical by the correspondence between the prefix sets and the essential redexes.
